claims.text: The initial nanoscale catalyst is a solid solution containing Pt, Pd, Rh, Ru, Ir, and Os.
Pt, Pd, Rh, Ru, Ir, and Os are uniformly distributed in the initial catalyst.
Increasing Ru concentration enhances ethanol-oxidation catalytic activity.
Increasing Ru concentration modifies the catalyst's electronic structure.
The Ru-induced electronic-structure modification improves electron-transfer kinetics.
The relevant structural mediator is the local electronic structure of Ru atoms in the catalyst lattice.
Higher Ru content alters the electronic properties of active sites.
The altered active-site electronic properties facilitate electron transfer.
The altered active-site electronic properties lower the activation barrier for ethanol oxidation.
Increasing Ru content up to about 10% will produce higher ethanol-oxidation current density than a catalyst with minimal or no Ru.
Increasing Ru content up to about 10% will produce a higher ethanol-oxidation reaction rate than a catalyst with minimal or no Ru.
The proposed Ru effect holds over the 0% to 10% Ru range in nanoscale solid-solution catalysts.
The proposed Ru effect holds during ethanol oxidation in acidic aqueous media at approximately 25–60 °C and ambient pressure.
The non-Ru metal proportions can be kept constant while the Ru concentration is increased from 0% to 10%.
Failure to observe any measurable activity increase relative to the low- or no-Ru baseline would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Increasing Ru atomic fraction while keeping every other metal's atomic fraction constant is incompatible with composition normalization. This becomes coherent only if 'constant' means that the other metals retain fixed ratios to one another while their absolute fractions decrease.

A 0% Ru endpoint is not literally a PtPdRhRuIrOs six-element catalyst and has no Ru atoms whose local electronic structure can serve as the stated mediator. It should be identified as a five-component control rather than as the same six-component system.
